title: Async kernel negotiation and NCCL slipstreaming for multi-GPU prefill/decode
creator: Sofia Liu
description:
Goal: Reduce 99th-percentile tail latency for multi-GPU prefill+decode workloads by enabling asynchronous kernel negotiation between stages and overlapping collective communication (NCCL) with opportunistic compute ('slipstreaming').

Background: Our current prefill/decode path serializes kernel selection and handoff logic across tensor- and pipeline-parallel stages which leads to stalled queues during dynamic sequence-length and batch-size variance. NCCL collectives are often scheduled conservatively, missing opportunities to run concurrently with adjacent attention kernels. This ticket prototypes a non-blocking kernel negotiation protocol (lightweight capability exchange) and a slipstreaming strategy that allows comms to start when partial readiness is detected while later compute continues, subject to correctness gates.

Success criteria / acceptance:
- End-to-end p99 latency for a 8-GPU OpenLlama-like workload reduced by >= 18% vs baseline for mixed-length inference (50/350 token mix).
- No correctness regressions on KV cache state, attention outputs, or past-key/value alignment across shards.
- CPU/GPU utilization increases by >= 12% during high-concurrency bursts (measured via trace sampling).
- Feature gated and can be rolled back per-model or per-deployment.

Design notes:
1) Negotiation handshake: lightweight metadata exchange at stage boundaries indicating (a) selected kernel variant id, (b) expected sequence length window, (c) readiness bitmap for shards. Handshake is piggybacked on existing control channel to avoid additional RPCs.
2) Slipstreaming policy: when a receiving stage reports partial readiness (>= 50% shards ready or expected prefill tokens below threshold), upstream stage may initiate an NCCL operation for KV exchange with a lower priority tag and continue issuing compute kernels that are safe to run speculatively (e.g., attention micro-tiles that do not depend on remaining shards).
3) Safety: speculative compute must be abortable. We add lightweight epoch stamps to KV ops; speculative results are validated after full NCCL completion. Mismatches trigger a deterministic replay for only the affected micro-tiles.
4) Kernel selection hints: kernel selector augments profiling table with a slipstream-suitability score (memory overlap tolerance, comm-to-compute ratio) so we choose kernels that minimize abort cost.
5) Telemetry: add trace spans for negotiation start/end, slipstream NCCL injections, speculative aborts, and replay counts. Provide per-model dashboard slices.

Implementation plan (Phases):
- Phase 1 (prototype): implement handshake metadata, basic slipstream NCCL initiation, and instrumentation. (Spike + microbench)
- Phase 2 (validation): integrate kernel selector hints, implement speculative compute abort and micro-tile replay, run deterministic correctness tests on small-model sharded setups.
- Phase 3 (canary): rollout to a subset of dedicated fleet for latency/throughput A/B tests; monitor telemetry for replays and errors.

Artifacts & links:
- Design doc (internal Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Async+Kernel+Negotiation+Design
- Spike benchmark notebook: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/u/0/folders/1sSlipstreamingSpikes
- Draft PR with proto handshake + traces: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4621

Compatibility & constraints:
- Feature gated at runtime via route-level config (console rollout).
- Works with tensor-parallel (1D) and pipeline-parallel configurations; for complex 2D sharding topologies we fallback to conservative behavior.
- Depends on NCCL >= 2.18 for non-blocking group progress on our infra; fallback path exists but with reduced overlap.

Rollout plan:
- Internal canary on dedicated staging cluster (4–8 GPUs) -> Dedicated canaries (selected customer routes) -> Gradual enabled by model label in console (runtime-1.20 release).

Notes on risks:
- Speculative abort rate could cause CPU overhead; we will gate slipstream threshold and add adaptive backoff.
- Interactions with autoscaling: ensure slipstreaming does not trigger spurious scale-ups; add token-level cost heuristics to console.
